content.title: Matching Chart Data with Textual Claims
content.overview: This lesson focuses on identifying and selecting chart data that directly supports or refutes a specific academic claim in a text. On the SAT, this requires students to not only read charts but also precisely locate the core argument within the passage.
learning_objectives: Identify specific academic claims or hypotheses in a text that require data support
Locate specific variables and values in a chart related to the textual claim
Evaluate whether selected data logically confirms or falsifies the claim in the text
Eliminate distractors that contain correct data but are irrelevant to the textual argument

sections.title: Identifying the Core Claim
sections.content: When approaching these questions, the first step is to read the stimulus text and find the 'claim' the author is trying to prove. Claims often appear at the end of the paragraph as a hypothesis, research finding, or prediction. For example, if a text discusses a certain plant growing faster at high temperatures, your goal is to find data showing a positive correlation between 'increased temperature' and 'increased growth rate'.

sections.title: Data Matching Strategy
sections.content:
Once the claim is identified, return to the chart to find the corresponding variables. Pay attention to the chart title, axis labels (X and Y axes), and the legend. Effective evidence must include all key variables mentioned in the claim. If a claim involves 'changes after 2010,' data from before 2010, no matter how accurate, cannot serve as direct evidence.

![Data and Claim Matching Process](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/74f9c5ba-7914-4e04-ab56-fa395ddc6212-1786502023893-951.webp)

sections.title: Logical Consistency Check
sections.content: Data supporting a claim must be consistent with the claim's trend. If the claim is 'A is more popular than B,' the correct option must reflect a higher value for A than B. If an option describes the relationship between C and D, or compares A and B on an unrelated dimension, it is a distractor.

worked_examples.question: Textual Claim: Researcher Li Hua believes that when light intensity exceeds 500 lux, the reproduction rate of this photosensitive bacteria significantly decreases. Based on this claim, which data would best support Li Hua's view?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the claim. The core variables are 'light intensity > 500' and 'reproduction rate decreases.' Step 2: Filter the data. Look for reproduction rates at light intensities of 600, 700, etc. Step 3: Verify the trend. If the data shows a reproduction rate of 80% at 400 lux but a drop to 30% at 600 lux, the data supports the claim. The correct answer should describe this specific numerical comparison showing a decrease in reproduction as light increases.

common_mistakes: Choosing a data point that exists in the chart but is irrelevant to the textual claim
Confusing the relationship between the independent variable (cause) and dependent variable (effect)
Ignoring qualifiers in the text, such as 'only under specific conditions' or 'significantly increased'
Selecting an option that describes a general trend in the chart but fails to address the specific details of the claim
exam_tips: Read the last sentence of the text first; the claim needing support is usually hidden there
Beware of the 'reverse support' trap: ensure the direction of the data trend (increase/decrease) matches the claim exactly
If the question asks to 'weaken' the claim, look for data that contradicts the predicted trend
Pay attention to unit conversions or the difference between percentages and absolute values to ensure the description matches the chart scale
content.recap: Matching chart data with textual claims requires students to build a logical bridge between 'understanding the argument' and 'extracting data.' The key to success is ensuring the selected data points perfectly align with the textual claim in terms of variables, timeframes, and trend direction.

knowledge_claims.content: A 'claim' is an academic viewpoint or hypothesis presented in a text that needs to be confirmed or falsified through quantitative evidence.
The primary step in solving these questions is to precisely locate the specific sentence in the text describing the research conclusion or prediction.
Effective evidence must involve the same variables mentioned in the textual claim, such as specific years, species, or physical quantities.
If a textual claim involves a positive correlation between two variables, supporting data must show both variables increasing or decreasing together.
A common error is selecting an option that is numerically correct according to the chart but irrelevant to the specific hypothesis discussed in the text.
Before selecting an option, check if the timeframe of the data matches the timeframe established by the textual claim.
Supporting evidence requires the data trend to match the claim, while weakening evidence requires the data trend to oppose the claim.
The legend in a chart is crucial for distinguishing between different experimental groups or categories and must correspond to the subjects in the text.
When a text mentions a 'significant difference,' the correct data option usually compares two data points with a clear numerical gap.
Even if an option describes a correct scientific fact, it is wrong if it does not directly cite data from the chart to support the textual claim.

items.stem: In 1534 CE, King Henry Vill of England split with the Catholic Church and declared himself head of the Church of England, in part because Pope Clement VII refused to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. Two years later, Henry VIll introduced a policy titled the Dissolution of the Monasteries that by 1540 had resulted in the closure of all Catholic monasteries in England and the confiscation of their estates. Some historians assert that the enactment of the policy was primarily motivated by perceived financial opportunities. Which quotation from a scholarly article best supports the assertion of the historians mentioned in the text?

options.A: "At the time of the Dissolution of the Monasteries, about 2 percent of the adult male population of England were monks; by 1690, the proportion of the adult male population who were monks was less than 1 percent."
options.B: "A contemporary description of the Dissolution of the Monasteries, Michael Sherbrook's Falle of the Religious Howses, recounts witness testimony that monks were allowed to keep the contents of their cells and that the monastery timber was purchased by local yeomen."
options.C: "In 1535, the year before enacting the Dissolution of the Monasteries, Henry commissioned a survey of the value of church holdings in England-the work, performed by sheriffs, bishops, and magistrates, began that January and was swiftly completed by the summer."
options.D: "The October 1536 revolt known as the Pilgrimage of Grace had several economic motives: high food prices due to a poor harvest the prior year; the Dissolution of the Monasteries, which closed reliable sources of food and shelter for many; and rents and taxes throughout Northern England that were not merely high but predatory."

items.explanation: The correct answer is C: "In 1535, the year before enacting the Dissolution of the Monasteries, Henry commissioned a survey of the value of church holdings in England-the work, performed by sheriffs, bishops, and magistrates, began that January and was swiftly completed by the summer.". Review the Exam Essentials and worked examples above, then apply the same reasoning to this question.

items.stem: Baltimore, Maryland, has installed engineered structures along 71% of its shoreline to protect infrastructure from wave erosion and other hazards, a practice known as shoreline hardening. To evaluate the responses of waterbirds to two types of hardening structures-riprap and bulkheads-Diann Prosser et al. surveyed waterbird communities consisting of the tundra swan, the great blue heron, and 62 other species at different sites in the Chesapeake Bay on the US East Coast. Utilizing the Index of Waterbird Community Integrity (IWCI), on which a high score corresponds to high community integrity, the researchers found that bulkheads are more strongly negatively correlated with waterbird community integrity than is riprap. Which finding, if true, would most directly illustrate the researchers' finding?

options.A: The difference in average IWCI scores for waterbird communities at Stony and Old Road, two sites with a higher percentage of shoreline consisting of bulkheads than of riprap, was statistically insignificant.
options.B: Waterbird communities at Old Road, a site with a relatively high percentage of shoreline consisting of bulkheads, had lower average IWCI scores than did waterbird communities at Miles, a site with a relatively high percentage of shoreline consisting of riprap.
options.C: Waterbird communities at Curtis, a site with a high percentage of shoreline consisting of bulkheads and riprap, had lower average IWCI scores than did waterbird communities at Onancock, a site with a low percentage of shoreline consisting of bulkheads and riprap.
options.D: Waterbird communities at Curtis, a site with equal percentages of shoreline consisting of bulkheads and riprap, had higher average IWCI scores than did waterbird communities at Miles, a site with different percentages of shoreline consisting of bulkheads and riprap.

items.explanation: The correct answer is B: Waterbird communities at Old Road, a site with a relatively high percentage of shoreline consisting of bulkheads, had lower average IWCI scores than did waterbird communities at Miles, a site with a relatively high percentage of shoreline consisting of riprap.. Review the Exam Essentials and worked examples above, then apply the same reasoning to this question.
